layout_dets.text: ABSTRACT

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In the evolving landscape of video editing methodologies, a majority of deep

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: learning techniques are often reliant on extensive datasets of observed input and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ground truth sequence pairs for optimal performance. Such reliance often falters

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: when acquiring data becomes challenging, especially in tasks like video dehazing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and relighting, where replicating identical motions and camera angles in both cor-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rupted and ground truth sequences is complicated. Moreover, these conventional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: methodologies perform best when the test distribution closely mirrors the training

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distribution. Recognizing these challenges, this paper introduces a novel video de-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: composition prior ‘VDP’framework which derives inspiration from professional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: video editing practices. Our methodology does not mandate task-specific exter-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nal data corpus collection, instead pivots to utilizing the motion and appearance

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the input video. VDP framework decomposes a video sequence into a set of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: multiple RGB layers and associated opacity levels. These set of layers are then

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: manipulated individually to obtain the desired results. We addresses tasks such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as video object segmentation, dehazing, and relighting. Moreover, we introduce a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: novel logarithmic video decomposition formulation for video relighting tasks, set-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ting a new benchmark over the existing methodologies. We evaluate our approach

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on standard video datasets like DAVIS, REVIDE, & SDSD and show qualitative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: results on a diverse array of internet videos.¹

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1 INTRODUCTION

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Deep learning techniques, prominently convolutional networks (Krizhevsky et al., 2012) and vi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sion transformers (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020), have emerged as the preferred choice for video-related

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tasks (Shrivastava & Shrivastava, 2024; Bodla et al., 2021; Shrivastava & Shrivastava, 2021; Saini

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: et al., 2022; Shrivastava, 2021) due to their superior results over the classical techniques. Typically,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: these frameworks are trained using a standardized method: curate a dataset of input/corrupted and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ground truth/clean sequences, design the model, and minimize the L2 loss between predictions and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: actual values. While this supervised approach sets state-of-the-art benchmarks, it grapples with two

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: significant challenges. First, collecting extensive datasets with annotated pairs for every task is im-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: practical and expensive. Second, as demonstrated by prior works like Shrivastava et al. (2023), the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: performance of pretrained models deteriorates when the test data slightly deviates from the training

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: data.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: To circumvent these challenges, emerging video editing methods (Lu et al., 2020a;b; 2021; Kasten

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: et al., 2021; Shrivastava et al., 2023) were developed and they offer three key advantages: they

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: operate directly on test sequences (also known as inference-time optimization), thereby obviating

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the need for collecting input and ground truth pairs; they are immune to dataset biases and generalize

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: well to unseen examples (Shrivastava et al., 2023); and they are resource-efficient as they do not have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to optimize over an external training corpus instead they optimize only on the given test input video.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: However, these techniques are not without limitations. They are often designed for very specific

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tasks, and they often perform inferior to their data-trained counterpart.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In this paper, we propose a inference-time optimization framework VDP, that does not rely on a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: collection of task-specific video input and ground truth sequence pairs. We took inspiration from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: professional video editing techniques – where sequences are broken down into multiple RGB layers.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Each RGB layer is associated with a distinct opacity layer, and by manipulating these RGB layers

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and their associated opacity levels, desired outcomes are achieved. In this work, we emphasize that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: proper decomposition formulation of a video leads to visually realistic solutions for the tasks. Fig. 1

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: illustrates our approach for the 3 different tasks discussed. Our framework relies only on the input

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: video and its derived optical flow to solve a wide variety of video-specific tasks.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: From a technical standpoint, VDP consists of two integral modules: RGB-Net' that operates on the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: appearance aspect of the input video and α-Net' that operates on the associated optical flow RGB

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the input video. Both of these modules are designed using the convolutional U-Net architec-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ture. Based on the tasks, we use the appropriate video decomposition formulation and appropriate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: regularization terms. We then jointly optimize these convolutional U-Nets for the same.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Our work makes three main contributions. 1) To the best of our knowledge we are the first approach

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to utilize FlowRGBs in an inference-time optimization technique to exploit the motion cues from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a query video. 2) We introduce a new formulation of the logarithmic decomposition of a video to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perform a relighting task. This new formulation leads to significant improvement in performance

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: when compared to the current baseline methods. 3) We achieve state-of-the-art performances on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relevant downstream applications of video decomposition, such as video dehazing and relighting.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: VDP outperforms the existing inference-time optimization techniques for video object segmentation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2 RELATED WORKS

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Traditionally, priors played a pivotal role in transforming an ill-posed problem'(one with multiple

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: plausible solutions) to a well-posed problem. Past proposed priors (Wang & Adelson, 1994; Shade

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: et al., 1998; Shechtman et al., 2002; 2005; He et al., 2010) were very limited in their capability of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: learning a good representation of videos to generalize well on various scenes. All of this changed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with the recent developments in deep learning techniques that considerably improve the representa-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion of videos and deliver high-performance gains on video editing tasks.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Established works such as (Assaf Shocher, 2018; Ulyanov et al., 2018; Bell-Kligler et al., 2019;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Pollak Zuckerman et al., 2020; Shrivastava et al., 2023) are test time optimization techniques, i.e.,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: they directly work on the corrupted input image/video sequences and do not require any ground

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: truth for training. These approaches have highlighted the importance of formulating a loss func-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for both image and video restoration problems. However, these insights predominantly catered to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: limited vision tasks such as denoising, super-resolution, and inpainting. Using our approach, we are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: able to address video relighting, dehazing, and unsupervised video object segmentation tasks. We

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: demonstrate this breadth of applications by leveraging the compositionality properties inherent in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: videos.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: DoubleDIP (Gandelsman et al., 2019) employs a similar strategy, but their convolutional framework

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relies heavily on the appearance of the video when optimizing a task objective. This becomes a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: limitation when working with videos, as motion plays a critical role alongside appearance. Our

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: method tackles this bottleneck by harnessing optical flow as a motion cue. This inclusion of optical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: flow not only captures motion effectively but also permits warping operations vital for downstream

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tasks such as edit propagation, an ability absent in DoubleDIP's decomposition framework.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Other inference-time optimization methodologies, such as (Kasten et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2021;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2020a; Bar-Tal et al., 2022) are very task-specific and utilize a singular form of video composition

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formulation, i.e., α-blending. Techniques like these are heavily reliant on user-generated masks or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: image-centric baselines. In contrast to these methods, our proposed method can tackle a wide vari-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ety of tasks. In addition, our framework does not rely on pretrained image segmentation networks,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thereby enhancing its robustness, especially when confronted with unfamiliar objects in videos.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Method (Ye et al., 2022) is another inference-time optimization technique that avoids the use of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pretrained image segmentation but encounters issues with objects whose appearances fluctuate over

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: time, perhaps due to shifts in lighting. Such a limitation arises from their approach of encapsulating

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an object's global appearance in videos into a single canonical texture layer. In contrast, our pro-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: posed methodology takes advantage of frame-by-frame appearance and motion cues, making our

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: model significantly more resilient to variations in lighting.

layout_dets.text: 7 CONCLUSION

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We have demonstrated in the paper how the layered decomposition could be applied to a wide

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: variety of downstream tasks. It is important to note that our model does not require any explicit

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: training, i.e., we optimize the parameters using the test sequence itself. Additionally, in this paper,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: we achieve state-of-the-art performances in downstream tasks such as UVOS (among the other test

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: time optimization techniques), dehazing, and relighting. We also demonstrated that the targeted

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: edits propagation can also be performed as a downstream task of UVOS. With the help of semantic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or perception cues, we believe our framework can also be extended for monocular depth estimation,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semantic segmentation, and other high-level vision tasks.

layout_dets.text: C.1 UVOS - SCENE WITH IRREGULAR OBJECTS

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In Fig. 8, we demonstrate that our method doesn't mandate the object to belong to a common cat-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: egory to achieve the correct decomposition. This is in stark contrast to other methods like that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (Kasten et al., 2021), which heavily relies on MaskRCNN or a user-input mask for video decomposi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion. This flexibility provides our approach with an advantage, allowing for precise video foreground

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (FG) and background (BG) edits and ensuring seamless propagation throughout the sequence.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: C.2 UVOS - LIGHTING CHANGES

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: It's notable that the efficacy of deformable sprites (Ye et al., 2022) tends to deteriorate in video

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sequences where the appearance of an object undergoes alterations due to shifts in lighting. This

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: decrement in performance emerges primarily because deformable sprites attempt to encapsulate an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: object's universal appearance using a singular canonical RGB texture. In contrast, our framework

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: operates by modeling video decomposition at an individual frame level. Such an approach amplifies

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the resilience of the object segmentation process against lighting modifications, a fact that is evident

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from Fig. 9.(a).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: precisely segregates the foreground from the background. Intriguingly, when the layer parameter is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: adjusted to 3, the model successfully isolates each person into their distinct layer while maintaining

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a separate layer for the background.
